questions.q: Which three tests does the lesson use to spot a task that's a good candidate for AI?
options: It's language-heavy, a first draft would help, and you can check the result
It's urgent, it involves numbers, and nobody else is available to help
It's creative, it's brand new to you, and the stakes are very high
It's repetitive, it takes hours, and you won't need to review the output
questions.explain: The best candidates are language-heavy, like writing, reading, explaining, planning or organizing. They also benefit from a first draft, and you can tell whether the output is good.

questions.q: Your prompt library has grown to 40 saved prompts, but you only ever use a few of them. What does the lesson suggest?
options: Keep adding more, since a bigger library covers more situations
Delete the library and write every prompt from scratch each time
Keep a short library of the prompts you actually use
Switch to a new assistant, since a fresh start will help
questions.explain: Collecting prompts you never use is a common mistake, and a short library you use beats a huge one you don't. The lesson suggests eight to twelve prompts for the things you do most.

questions.q: You keep fixing the same problem in the answers from one of your saved prompts. What should you do?
options: Keep fixing it by hand, since saved prompts shouldn't change
Ask AI to improve the prompt, keeping it short with the brackets
Stop using that prompt and type a new one from scratch each time
Try a different assistant each time until one gets it right
questions.explain: When you notice you're fixing the same thing every time, improve the prompt. Paste it along with the usual issues and ask AI to improve it, keeping it short and keeping the brackets.
